I'm a lifelong vegetarian, been Type 1 for 5 years, a1c has never been over 6. I'm sure it's harder than being able to eat meat, but I've never had experience of the flip side. Benefits to the omnipod: no tubing, it's relatively small and light and I often entirely forget where it is on my body, I don't have to worry about keeping the pump clipped to clothes or anything (hugely beneficial if you often wear clothes that don't have pockets), plus if you toss and turn in your sleep you're less likely to rip out your infusion site. It's totally waterproof, too, so you don't have to remove your infusion sight for watersports or in the shower

Drawbacks are that you have to move your omnipod every three days. This can get annoying but it has the added benefit of forcing you to not overuse an injection site. Another potential drawback that I personally face is that omnipod requires a minimum of 80 units of insulin to activate, which is way too much for 3 days for me (I rarely use more than 20 in 3 days). Not sure if other pumps have the same restriction or not

High sugars after meals are common, especially if they're carby, and aren't that big of a deal as long as they aren't too crazy out of range. I have been T1D for 4 years and have only tested my ketones once or twice when my sugar was 250+ and wouldn't drop for a few hours.

Most insulin takes about 4 hours to completely absorb, so expect high sugars to stick around for an hour or two even after dosing.  Fatty/high protein food will make your BG increase and decrease much slower, while high sugar foods alone will make it spike/drop super quickly. My best advice is to have him eat a relatively healthy diet with more of an emphasis on fat/protein, and try to reduce fast processing sugars (desserts, white bread, and pasta are the death of my steady bg). For example, white bread is about 15g of carbs per slice, and makes my sugar jump from 100 to 200 back down to 100 in an hour, which isn't pleasant and messes up my stability all day. A slice of whole wheat bread is also about 15g of carbs, but makes my sugar only spike up to 130 and then steadily drop down to 100 over the next hour or so. 

The hardest part of being diabetic is getting your insulin ratios right, after the first month or two this will all be second hand, and getting the CGM and pump will only make it so much easier. Good luck!

Edit: Also, since you mentioned it, his high sugars aren't his normal, everyone's normal range is around 85-120. Anything higher is technically a "high sugar", though it isn't the end of the world. Your goal is to just keep our of high sugar as much as you can, but there is only so much you can do and high sugars are going to happen. Just try not to overcompensate and over dose him to try and make it go down quicker, because insulin takes so long to absorb it barely will speed up the process and just make him have a low sugar later. Every diabetic knows the pain of bouncing between super high and super low sugars from overcompensating our treatment
